Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sanhedrin 46a: ‘Rabbi Meir said: The phrase “for he that is hung is a curse [kilelat] of God” should be understood as follows: When a man suffers in the wake of his sin, what expression does the Divine Presence use? Mighty act (Gevurah) pertains to the arm, while praise (Tehillah) pertains to wisdom, for praise represents the honor of acclaim, and it is said: "The wise shall inherit honor" [Proverbs 3:35], and wisdom resides in the head, within the brain.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 17a: ‘Rava was wont to say: The objective of Torah wisdom is to achieve repentance and good deeds; that one should not read the Torah and study mishna and become arrogant and spurn his father and his mother and his teacher and one who is greater than he in wisdom or in the number of students who study before him, as it is stated: “The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord, a good understanding have all who fulfill them” (Psalms 111:10). Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Yet it appears that this applies only when his intention is purely self-serving—seeking personal bliss, longevity, and comfort in the hereafter, for which there is no functional difference between an earthly prize and a heavenly prize; whereas the true essence of the World to Come, which is that "they delight in the radiance of the Divine Presence" (Berakhot 17a), is not self-indulgent pleasure, and even in this world, whoever merits this experiences that single hour of repentance and good deeds which is sweeter than all the World to Come (Avot 4), where "the reward of a mitzvah is the mitzvah itself,"

This is why the Torah mentions Shabbat immediately before the work of the Mishkan, for the principle of their union was from the mitzvah of Shabbat, for Shabbat is included in all the mitzvot when one has the intention that they are for the sake of Heaven.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Taanit 31a: ‘It is taught that those women of distinguished lineage among them would say: Young man, please lift up your eyes and see what you choose for a wife. So it is said, “a woman who conceives,” meaning one who has true desire, with strength and vigor, for God.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ecclesiastes 7:1: ‘A good name is better than fragrant oil, and the day of death than the day of birth.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:20, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Ecclesiastes 7:1) to illuminate his teaching here (“We would not know which name is superior: that which he earned for himself or that given by his parents; King Solomon came and resolved: "and the day of death than the day of one's birth" Ecclesiastes 7:1, in the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And regarding the adage: "In my town, my reputation (shemi)," the "name" denotes the soul, as it is said (Genesis 2:19): "whatever the man called every living creature, that was the name thereof," the name hinting at that specific soul-potency; and as it is said (Ecclesiastes 7:1): "A good name is better than precious oil, and the day of death than the day of one's birth," "name" alluding to the purity of the soul akin to the day of death when the soul departs the body and no longer requires physical mitzvah performance, which is hinted at by good oil (Vayikra Rabbah 3).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Sod Yesharim, Parashat Parah 6:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “This is the statute of the Torah” (Numbers 19:2): Solomon said, “I said I will get wisdom, but it is far from me” (Ecclesiastes 7:23), and in Rosh Hashanah 21b our Sages taught that Kohelet sought to judge without witnesses and warning through pure wisdom until a heavenly voice proclaimed that no prophet arises like Moses. Even the highest human wisdom must bow before the supra-rational decree of the Torah transmitted through Moses.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 153a: ‘Rabbi Elazar raised a dilemma before Rav: Which type of person has a share in the World-to-Come? He said to him: We can derive this from the verse: “And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying: This is the path, walk on it, when you turn to the right or to the left” (Isaiah 30:21). In other words, if people eulogize one by saying that others should follow in his path, he must have a share in the World-to-Come. Rabbi Ḥanina said: Anyone with whom our Rabbis are pleased has a share in the World-to-Come. In interpreting the verse: “And the eulogizers walk about the marketplace” (Ecclesiastes 12:5), the people of the Galilee say: Do things that you will want people to say at your…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:20, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 153a) to illuminate his teaching here (“in the vein of the Sages Shabbat 153a: Act so that good deeds be recounted after your bier, for on the day of death it is his self-acquired name of righteousness that endures.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: All actions and spiritual labors are recognized only at the end, as written in Shabbat 153a: Who is destined for the World to Come? "And your ears shall hear a word behind you, etc." (Isaiah 30:21); and as long as the endeavor is not completed, it remains hidden from the sight of all, even from the person himself, such that even if he appears righteous and the entire world tells him "you are righteous," he must still view himself with humble vigilance (Niddah 30b), and likewise the reverse, for every matter is judged according to its ultimate outcome.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Talmud, Yoma 75a
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Care in the heart of a man bows it down (yashchenah)” (Proverbs 12:25): Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi expounded—one said, let him banish it from his mind, and the other said, let him speak of it to others. And concerning the manna (Yoma 75a): just as the manna descended each day requiring fresh trust in the Blessed Name for that day’s sustenance, so too every anxiety in the heart is meant to turn a person’s eyes upward in prayer and conversation before his Creator.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 152a: ‘The Gemara continues interpreting verses from Ecclesiastes. The verse states: “Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high and terrors shall be on the road, and the almond tree shall blossom, and the grasshopper shall drag itself along, and the caper berry shall fail, for a person goes to his eternal home, and the mourners circle the marketplace” (Ecclesiastes 12:5). The Gemara explains: “Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high”; this means that even a small knoll on the road seems to him, the elderly, like the highest of mountains. “And terrors shall be on the road”; this means that while he is walking on the road he will have terrors, i.e., he will fear falling or…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:21, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 152a) to illuminate his teaching here (“In Shabbat 152a: Rav Chisda stated: In my poverty of Torah I ate no greens—alluding to mitzvot that can be performed by others, which drag out much time and cause neglect of Torah study; "in my wealth... in the place...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Meaning that the interior of the heart and the depth of wisdom of each person differ one from another. And therefore they expounded (Shemot Rabbah 52) on the verse "man goes to his long home (beit olamo, the home of his world)" (Ecclesiastes 12:5), that every person possesses an entire world of his own; and this is what they termed elsewhere (Shabbat 152a): each person has a dwelling according to his honor, and as written in the Tikkunim (beginning of Tikkun 69) that "his own world" denotes his individual microcosm.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Mishpatim 1:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And these are the laws that you shall place before them ….” (Shemot, 21:1)Here it is not said, “And God spoke to Moshe saying,” as with all the mitzvot, for the matter here discusses civil legal enactments (“mishpatim”), and concerning justice there is no difference between the great and the small. This may be compared to when the king goes out to inspect and judge his soldiers; then they all stand in the same line, even their senior officer standing in the line.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sotah 2a: ‘The Gemara asks: Is that so that a man is matched to a woman according to his actions? But Rav Yehuda says that Rav says: Forty days before an embryo is formed a Divine Voice issues forth and says: The daughter of so-and-so is destined to marry so-and-so; such and such a house is destined to be inhabited by so-and-so; such and such a field is destined to be farmed by so-and-so. This clearly states that these matters, including marriage, are decreed for a person even before he is formed. The Gemara answers: This is not difficult. This statement that Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav is with regard to a first match [zivug], while this statement of Rabba bar bar Ḥana in the name of Rabbi…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:22, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 2a) to illuminate his teaching here (“"The daughter of so-and-so is destined for so-and-so" Sotah 2a, and not "so-and-so female for so-and-so," nor "the son of so-and-so"; in Mechir Yayin on Esther 2:2 it is noted that typically the conception of the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: All acquisitions belonging to a person are fundamentally attached to him from inception and rooted in his soul's origin, as stated at the beginning of Sotah [2a] that a heavenly voice proclaims prior to formation: "The daughter of so-and-so to so-and-so," and likewise "The field of so-and-so to so-and-so," for possessions also mirror marital pairing, possessing a predetermined bond at their root.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Tiferet Yosef, Bereshit 4:3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “One beyond number” refers to that which is entirely above the grasp of creation; and “One within number” refers to His manifestation within the framework of creation. And this is what the Midrash asks: “If it is according to the count of days,” meaning since creation has already begun here, it ought to have said “a first day” [in series]; and the Midrash answers: Rather, from the time when the Holy One, blessed be He, was completely alone in His world, He yearned to possess a dwelling place among the lower realms.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Esther 2:2: ‘The king’s servants who attended him said, “Let beautiful young virgins be sought out for Your Majesty.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:22, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Esther 2:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“in Mechir Yayin on Esther 2:2 it is noted that typically the conception of the groom precedes the bride, though the reason was left unexplained; and to me it seems: because a father holds legal authority to contract...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And based upon this the Midrash in Megillah (13a) teaches: "she had a greenish complexion, but a thread of divine lovingkindness was drawn over her"; and even though it is written "and the maiden was of beautiful form" (Esther 2:7), she was not the fairest of all. And so it is implied from Bava Batra (15b): "Job lived in the days of Ahasuerus, for it is said: 'and in all the land were no women found so fair as the daughters of Job' (Iyov 42:15)"; for was not Esther found more fair than they?! Rather, perforce, Esther found unearned grace (chen).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 7:6
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For this reason Israel is dispersed among the nations in order that they may receive all the powers residing in each of the seventy nations, and once in Israel it will be without limit. Thus it is written concerning King Shlomo (Bava Metsia, 86b), “He took wives from many nations,” for the strength of each nation is principally in its women, and particularly in the princess.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Batra 110a: ‘§ The mishna teaches in the list of those who inherit from and bequeath to each other: Sons with regard to their father. The Gemara asks: From where do we derive this halakha that sons inherit the entire estate and daughters do not receive a share along with them? As it is written: “If a man dies, and has no son, then you shall pass his inheritance to his daughter” (Numbers 27:8). The reason the inheritance would be passed to a daughter is that he has no son, but if he has a son, the son takes precedence. Rav Pappa said to Abaye: Why not say the following: If there is only a son, let the son inherit the father’s estate; if there is only a daughter, let the daughter inherit the father’s…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:22, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 110a) to illuminate his teaching here (“or because the Sages instructed a man to marry the daughter of worthy lineage, investigating her brothers Bava Batra 110a, whereas a woman is content with any partner: "better to dwell as two than as a widow" Yevamot...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is what our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Bava Batra 110a) on the verse "and Shebuel son of Gershom, son of Manasseh, was overseer of the treasuries" (I Chronicles 26:24): once David saw that money was exceedingly beloved to him, he appointed him over the treasuries, etc. Now behold, the treasuries were not his personal property, and David did not give him the treasuries at all, so how did this satisfy his craving?
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Re'eh 10
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And you shall rejoice before Hashem your God, you and sons and daughters and servants, and the Levi who is within your gates, and the stranger, and the orphan, and the widow who are among you, in the place that Hashem your God chooses to cause his name to dwell there.” (Devarim, 16:11)With all the other festivals it is written, “within your gates,”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yevamot 118b: ‘The Gemara states: From the fact that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said that Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva do not disagree with regard to the cases of one who betrothed and one who purchased, one may learn by inference that the first tanna, with whom he disagrees, holds that they do disagree about the cases of betrothed and purchased, whereas with regard to one who had sexual intercourse and one who stole an item Rabbi Tarfon agrees with Rabbi Akiva. With this in mind, who is the author of the mishna?’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:22, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yevamot 118b) to illuminate his teaching here (“or because the Sages instructed a man to marry the daughter of worthy lineage, investigating her brothers Bava Batra 110a, whereas a woman is content with any partner: "better to dwell as two than as a widow" Yevamot...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: After the manner they said [in Yevamos 118b]: "She says: 'Let my soul die with the Philistines!' (Shoftim 16:30)"; and [the Rosh] also wrote merely that it is "like spite," yet there is no logical ground for this, since in any event he acts solely to satisfy his personal desire and not to spite his Creator. And furthermore it appears that this ruling is astonishing from Sanhedrin [43b], that all who are executed confess; and since he confessed and repented, even though it was at the moment of death, certainly one must no longer reckon him as an apostate out of spite!
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Bereshit 11
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And the man said: The woman whom You gave to be with me, she gave me, etc. For in truth the mistake of Adam the First in his sin sprouted from this: because Hashem, blessed be He, said: "I will make him a help meet for him", inasmuch as when Adam was forbidden to eat from the tree of knowledge he feared greatly, for he reasoned: surely Hashem, blessed be He, forbade this to me only because He knows that there is a deficiency within me; yet when Hashem, blessed be He, created Eve for him and gave her to him as a help, meaning that he should follow her opinion, as was said to Abraham our father, peace be upon him (Genesis 21:12): "Whatever Sarah says to you…

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: [derived from "inheritance" (morashah [Deuteronomy 33:4]), inheritance being an inborn legacy transmitted from parents without personal effort; and likewise "betrothed" (me'orasah) reflects innate destiny, as taught in Sotah (2a): forty days before the formation of the fetus, etc.], the intent being that the Torah is not inherently theirs at all.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Tazria 3:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “A woman who conceives and gives birth to a man-child, she shall be unclean for seven days ….” (Vayikra, 12:2)We can understand the reason for this impurity with a parable. One comes with a request before a king, and writes his request on a crumpled scrap of paper. Even though he requested properly, and deserved what he had requested, and also the king answered him favorably, nonetheless, the king commands that he be imprisoned because he wrote his request on such a scrap of paper.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Leviticus 26:5: ‘Your threshing shall overtake the vintage, and your vintage shall overtake the sowing; you shall eat your fill of bread and dwell securely in your land.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:23, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Leviticus 26:5) to illuminate his teaching here (“"And you shall eat your bread to the full" Leviticus 26:5—that you gorged not in drunkenness, lest you sin; lest you object: "if there is no peace, abundance is worthless," lest anger flare and cause sin—Scripture...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: "I know only [that it applies] in the Land (Sifrei Zuta, cited in Yalkut Shimoni), which is the place of sacrifices and the place of atonement; whence do we derive that one confesses outside the Land? Scripture states (Leviticus 26:40): 'And they shall confess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers'" — that is to say, the iniquity of their fathers who sinned and were expelled from the Land; thus we learn that one confesses even outside the Land.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Bechukotai 1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “If you walk in My statutes (be-chukotai)” (Leviticus 26:3)—which the Sifra explains as “that you shall labor closely in the Torah”: when a person’s toil in Torah engraves (chakikah) the words of God into the very substance of his heart, even his natural walking and bodily habits become expressions of the divine will.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Leviticus 26:6: “And I will give peace in the land, and you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid; and I will cause evil beasts to cease out of the land, neither shall the sword go through your land.” Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:23, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Leviticus 26:6) to illuminate his teaching here (“lest you object: "if there is no peace, abundance is worthless," lest anger flare and cause sin—Scripture immediately adds: "And I will give peace in the land" ibid. 26:6; or according to Gittin 70a: fill only...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And so "and you shall perish (va-avadtem) among the nations" (Vayikra 26:38), expounded in Makkot (24a): like a lost object that is sought after, signifying not extinction but disappearance; and ultimately: "and they that were lost in the land of Assyria shall come, etc." (ibid.). And Haman was the historical initiator of decrees of religious apostasy (shemad); wherefore the Sages stated (Megillah 12a): Israel was condemned because they bowed down to the golden image in the days of Nebuchadnezzar, not sacrificing their lives for the sanctification of the Divine Name.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 61:19–21
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For the filling-letters equal Chavah, and the root letters themselves were taken from him, leaving him with only the filling on its own; and initially the filling was enfolded within the primary letters of the divine Name, on account of which he was compelled to humble himself in order to elevate her. And as it is written (Leviticus 26:11): “And I will set My dwelling (mishkani) among you,” upon which the Zohar expounds (Bechukotai 114a): “My pledge (mashkoni) is with you” —.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Gittin 70a: ‘§ Elijah the prophet said to Rabbi Natan: Eat a third of your fill, and drink a third of your fill, and leave a third of your fill, so that when you become angry you will become full. If you do this, there will be room, as it were, for the anger. If you become angry when your stomach is full you will be harmed.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:23, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Gittin 70a) to illuminate his teaching here (“or according to Gittin 70a: fill only one-third of the stomach, so that if anger strikes, digestion does not rupture; hence if one eats to repletion without peace, no blessing resides therein:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: So that even if he cannot conquer it through Torah reflection (unholy thoughts disturbing his study); the preceding derech eretz remains to subdue it through natural moral decency. And so even when the yetzer deceives him into thinking his frequent intimacy is for the sake of Heaven to dispel stray thoughts; according to his perspective he acts within derech eretz, wherefore it is called "like roosters" regarding natural conduct; yet it is derogatory, being merely the way of physical man without holiness!
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Noach 16:9–11
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And only afterward may he receive it, where it is considered as bought with payment, having earned it through the toil of momentary self-restraint. As the Sages taught in Gittin (70a): “From a meal in which you take pleasure, withdraw your hand”; meaning: pause to reflect whether the pleasure aligns with the divine Will or not.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sanhedrin 26a: ‘Hezekiah was afraid. Meaning, it is a conspiracy of wicked people, and a conspiracy of wicked people is not counted. Therefore, although they are many, they are not considered the majority.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:24, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 26a) to illuminate his teaching here (“When two negative quantities combine, their union remains negative, matching: "a conspiracy of the wicked does not count in the reckoning" Sanhedrin 26a. And if positive and negative forces combine: if the positive...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.

[ibid. 12:26]— that was Hashem's spontaneous promise, and from the Most High evil proceeds not, an enduring chain of goodness being destined to emerge from them, as Isaiah rebuked Hezekiah (Berakhot 10a): "Why do you meddle in the secrets of the Merciful One?".

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 32:5: ‘and instructed them as follows, “Thus shall you say, ‘To my lord Esau, thus says your servant Jacob: I stayed with Laban and remained until now;’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:24, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 32:5) to illuminate his teaching here (“And if positive and negative forces combine: if the positive forces predominate, the composite remains positive, as Jacob declared: "I have sojourned with Laban" and observed the 613 mitzvot without being corrupted...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Through which "He delivered our houses" (Shemos 12:27), the skipping occurring over the houses which form the surrounding enclosure; for in that outer boundary evil touches the souls of Israel through immersion; yet they were rescued through the blood of the Pesach, which is the total surrender of their animal soul (the blood) unto the Blessed Name; this being the inner meaning of sprinkling sacrificial blood as is known; and through this it became impossible for evil to touch them from the outside, and "no plague shall come near your tent" (Tehillim 91:10).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayishlach 7
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the dawn” (Genesis 32:25). Throughout the night of this world, the guardian angel of Esau wrestles with Jacob by casting doubts and obscuring the clarity of his heart; yet precisely through standing firm in that struggle until the dawn of redemption, Jacob merits the name Israel, ‘for you have striven with God and with men and have prevailed.’

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Exodus 12:27: ‘you shall say, ‘It is the passover sacrifice to GOD, who passed over the houses of the Israelites in Egypt when smiting the Egyptians, but saved our houses.’”Those assembled then bowed low in homage.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:24, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Exodus 12:27) to illuminate his teaching here (“And if positive and negative forces combine: if the positive forces predominate, the composite remains positive, as Jacob declared: "I have sojourned with Laban" and observed the 613 mitzvot without being corrupted...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And we find "and the people bowed their heads and worshipped" in Parashat Bo (Exodus 12:27), where Rashi explains: they rejoiced over the tidings of future children; yet there it is framed in the question "What is this service to you?", which is the question of the wicked son as brought in the Haggadah: "you too blunt his teeth, etc.", and even so, they rejoiced over the tidings of his birth.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Sod Yesharim, The First Night of Pesach 4:2
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Why was the Exodus from Egypt accompanied by haste (chipazon), as written: ‘You shall eat it in haste’ (Exodus 12:11) and ‘In haste you went forth from the land of Egypt’ (Deuteronomy 16:3), whereas of the future redemption it is said: ‘For you shall not go forth in haste’ (Isaiah 52:12)? At the Exodus from Egypt, Israel’s outer garments of body and nature were not yet fully refined, so the supernal light had to rescue them abruptly before the appointed time; in the future redemption, every vessel will be completely purified to receive the light in tranquil permanence.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Psalms 106:35: ‘but mingled with the nationsand learned their ways.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:24, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Psalms 106:35) to illuminate his teaching here (“but if negative forces predominate, the composite turns negative: "they mingled themselves with the nations, and learned their works" Psalms 106:35, and: "along with the thorn the cabbage is struck" Bava Kamma 92a,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.

And therefore the righteous person is caught, and "along with the thorn the cabbage is struck" (Bava Kamma 92a); and certainly all is in true judgment, operating as noted above, because he inadvertently consented and triggered their punishment, and therefore it begins with him, as stated in Bava Kamma 92a, parallel to the benevolent measure: "He who prays for his fellow is answered first" (Bava Kamma 92a).

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: The Holy One, blessed be He, answered him that the portion of Jacob was different from the rest of the world. It is the way of the nations that when they see a major change in the management of the world, then they begin to amend their ways and want to understand the reason for the change. Yet when the world runs according to the way of nature (without any apparent changes), then none among them take it upon themselves to understand, for they do not believe in God to the extent that the ways of nature are also in His hands.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As stated (Psalms 12:1): “For the Leader; upon the Sheminith. A Psalm of David”— upon circumcision which was commanded for the eighth day; and this commandment abides continually with man even in a state lacking all conscious awareness. “And I will be their God”— meaning: even though he will possess all bounties, he nonetheless will never forget Hashem, blessed be He; and it is consonant with what is taught in the Talmud (Bava Kamma 92b): “The wine belongs to the host, but gratitude is accorded to the server”.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: II Chronicles 20:37: ‘Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, “As you have made a partnership with Ahaziah, GOD will break up your work.” The ships were wrecked and were unable to go to Tarshish.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:24, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (II Chronicles 20:37) to illuminate his teaching here (“but if negative forces predominate, the composite turns negative: "they mingled themselves with the nations, and learned their works" Psalms 106:35, and: "along with the thorn the cabbage is struck" Bava Kamma 92a,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.

And Scripture warns: "My son, walk not in the way with them" (Proverbs 1:15), and everywhere the word "way" (derekh) in Proverbs signifies the path of Torah and commandments.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Writings, Proverbs 16
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “The arrangements of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the Lord… The Lord has made everything for His purpose, yes, even the wicked for the day of evil” (Proverbs 16:1, 4). Even the opposing forces in creation were formed solely to clarify and elevate the heart of man, so that through overcoming them he recognizes that every step is guided by the Blessed Name.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this was the Exodus from Egypt, Israel having descended thither on account of food and due to famine; and as long as a single one of the tribal Patriarchs survived, who were entirely a seed of truth, the Egyptians were unable to enslave them or impose upon them the yoke of government and worldly labor; because the yoke of Torah rested upon them; until subsequently when they sank into the unholy shell of Egypt; the entire power of this husk being to submerge man in the materialistic affairs of this world.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Matot 6:3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Pinchas saw his mistake and killed him, as is explained there, for God did not choose this matter to come about this way in the world. Here Moshe Rabeynu showed Pinchas that he is now making the same mistake in letting the Midianites live, as it erroneously occurred to him that he could bring them into a state of Kedusha. For here they did not actually see the action (as with Zimri), and it seemed to Pinchas that they would be permitted to live, yet Moshe Rabeynu understood that at the depths they are forbidden.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Exodus 5:9: ‘Let heavier work be laid upon those involved; let them keep at it and not pay attention to deceitful promises.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Exodus 5:9) to illuminate his teaching here (“"Let heavier work be laid upon the men..." ibid. 5:9, hence: "and let them not regard lying words"—empty hopes, for I shall grant no respite. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Only that upon the death of Joseph and that entire generation, when it became possible that they might sink into the delusions of Egypt, Heaven decreed the harsh servitude and bodily toil in worldly labor, which also serves to purge the memory of sin. For the root of delusions arises from idleness, which leads to sin. But when one is absorbed in work, the mind concentrates on the task that it be done properly, and this was an unavoidable focus for them since they were coerced into it.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Mishpatim 4:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Six days shall you do your work, and on the seventh day you shall rest ….” (Shemot, 23:12)In Parshat Yitro, when discussion Shabbat, it uses the opposite order; “remember the day of Shabbat to keep it holy,” and then afterwards, “six days shall you work,” etc. We can understand this from the Gemara (Shabbat, 69b), “if one is wandering in the desert, and does not know when the day of Shabbat is, Hiya bar Rav says, he shall keep one day of Shabbat, and then count six.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Exodus 5:2: ‘But Pharaoh said, “Who is GOD that I should heed him and let Israel go? I do not know GOD, nor will I let Israel go.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:25, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Exodus 5:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“And the Egyptians did not recognize the Tetragrammaton, as Pharaoh professed: "Who is Hashem...?" ibid. 5:2; therefore Pharaoh initially cited their words: "they are idle... to our God Eloheinu," yet subsequently...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And even Pharaoh's defiance: "Who is Hashem that I should obey His voice?", having been inscribed in the Torah, reflects his vital root wherein God embedded this challenge, for cosmic concealment likewise proceeds from Hashem's essential will in Creation: first darkness and then light (Shabbat 77b); and "forming light and creating darkness" Isaiah 45:7, creation (Beri'ah) being an exalted realm, darkness stemming from a deeper divine desire that darkness serve a purpose.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Beshalach 1:3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: There are times when God hides His actions and conceals His intentions from mankind. Then man does not know God’s will is in that particular matter, as we find in our case where Moses was uncertain, a wonder in his view why God did not lead the people through the land of the Philistines.If one sees that God is dealing with him in a hidden, inscrutable way, then he is advised not to be too clever, but should rather perform the mitzvot with simplicity and intensify his fear of God.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Wherefore horses originated from Egypt, where began the power of dominating others in crushing bondage; whence no slave could ever escape (Rashi on Shemos 18:9 from Mechilta); Pharaoh boasting: "Who is Hashem, that I should obey His voice to let Israel go?" (Shemos 5:2); imagining himself supreme, no power capable of overcoming him; their monarch deified: "My river is my own, and I have made it for myself" (Yechezkel 29:3).

As expounded in Chullin 89a: the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel, ‘I love you because even when I bestow greatness upon you, you diminish yourselves before Me’—as Abraham said ‘I am dust and ashes,’ and Moses and Aaron said ‘What are we?’

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Wherefore the future eschatological test of the idolaters will be through the mitzvah of Sukkah (Avodah Zarah 3a); for this applies exclusively unto "the native-born in Israel" (Vayikra 23:42); whereas the nations are utterly incapable of bearing anything other than a permanent dwelling and a rigid structure; and this is why they reckon by the sun (Sukkah 29a) which has fixed permanence, for "the sun knows its going down" (Tehillim 104:19); whereas the moon knows not its going down, its circuit being sometimes long and sometimes short (Rosh Hashanah 25a), having no static permanence.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sukkah 29a: ‘If, during an eclipse, the visage of the sun is red like blood, it is an omen that sword, i.e., war, is coming to the world. When it is similar both to this, to blood, and to that, to sackcloth, it is a sign that both sword and arrows of hunger are coming to the world. If it was eclipsed upon its entry, soon after rising, it is an omen that calamity is tarrying to come. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is the beginning of the entry of a Jewish man into the service of the Blessed Name through the Torah; which is an acquired inheritance in his heart; and it is "the portal" (tar'a); and through this he enters unto "the inner dwelling" (darta), which is fear of Heaven; for "this is the whole man," as stated at the conclusion of Koheles (12:13): "The end of the matter, all having been heard: fear God, and keep His commandments; for this is the whole man"; and as it is said: "And now, Israel, what does Hashem your God require of you, but to fear Hashem your God" (Devarim 10:12).

This matter defies logic, for if a thousand Gentiles stand with one Israelite among them, the form of the Israelite will be recognized, and this is a wonder in the eyes of all the whole world.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sanhedrin 21b: ‘And Rabbi Yitzḥak says: For what reason were the rationales of Torah commandments not revealed? It was because the rationales of two verses were revealed, and the greatest in the world, King Solomon, failed in those matters. It is written with regard to a king: “He shall not add many wives for himself, that his heart should not turn away” (Deuteronomy 17:17). Solomon said: I will add many, but I will not turn away, as he thought that it is permitted to have many wives if one is otherwise meticulous not to stray. And later, it is written: “For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods” (I Kings 11:4).’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:27, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 21b) to illuminate his teaching here (“whereas if reasons are revealed, human conceit stumbles, as King Solomon rationalized: "I will multiply wives and not turn aside" Sanhedrin 21b:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: The Zohar then relates that wisdom was given to King Shlomo. Shlomo said, in effect, 'God and His wisdom are with me, and I can act as I wish,' corresponding to 'I shall increase [wives] and will not stray' (Sanhedrin 21b). This confidence came from his supernal wisdom. One view in Rosh Hashanah 21b says that 'no prophet arose like Moshe' excludes prophets, but one did arise among kings; nevertheless Shlomo relied upon that wisdom and declared, 'I shall increase and not stray.'
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayetzei 9:3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For it is not enough to reveal the light of the king messiah in the merit of the Patriarchs, only for the sake of His name. This is as it is written in the Gemara (Sanhedrin, 100a), “whoever gives the poor his entire amount in this world, the Holy One, blessed be He, gives him His entire amount in the world to come.” Because they exerted themselves with all their power, that the glory of Heaven should be revealed by means of them, therefore the attribute of justice dictates that the Holy One, blessed be He, should pay them according to the full amount of His blessed power.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 88a: ‘Ḥizkiya said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “You caused sentence to be heard from heaven; the earth feared, and was silent” (Psalms 76:9)? If it was afraid, why was it silent; and if it was silent, why was it afraid? It is said (Bereshit Rabba, 45:8), “when Sarah became pregnant, many infertile women in the world became pregnant at the same time.” In response to this, many of the scoffers of the generation said, “who is to say that this miracle came about through the power of Sarah, were not many other infertile women answered with children?”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yevamot 64a: ‘Abba Ḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer: A man who does not engage in procreation is liable to death, as it is stated with regard to the sons of Aaron: “And Nadav and Avihu died…and they had no children” (Numbers 3:4). This indicates that if they would have had children they would not have died. Others say: He causes the Divine Presence to depart from the Jewish people, as it is stated: “To be a God to you and to your seed after you” (Genesis 17:7). When your seed is after you, i.e., when you have children, the Divine Presence rests upon the Jewish people, but if your seed is not after you, upon whom can the Divine Presence rest? Upon wood and stones?’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:46, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yevamot 64a) to illuminate his teaching here (““And they dwelled there about ten years” Ruth 1:4, as in Yevamot 64a: ten barren years abroad stems from the sin of foreign exile, serving as an unheeded warning to return, wherefore they died:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And that mountain is called Mount Moriah after myrrh (mor), as is known (Bereishit Rabbah 55), which is the foremost of all spices (Megillah 10b), a matter of distinction and not ownerless for all to take. So too is service of the heart, which is prayer, as they taught in Yevamot (64a): "The prayer of a righteous person born of a righteous person does not compare to the prayer of a righteous person born of a wicked person," and they did not mean regarding the reception of the prayer through ancestral merit.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Kedoshim 1:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And God spoke to Moshe saying: Speak to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, and say to them, be holy, for I am holy, Hashem, your God.” (Vayikra, 19:1–2)“The congregation of the children of Israel” means any place where Israel gathers together for the sake of Heaven, as it is written in the Gemara (Sanhedrin, 38b), “whenever ten Jews gather together, the Shechina [Divine Presence] rests on them.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ruth Rabbah 2:10: ‘“Both of them died, Maḥlon and Kilyon, and the woman was bereft of her two children and of her husband” (Ruth 1:5).“Both of them died, Maḥlon and Kilyon.” Rabbi Ḥunya, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Rabbi Avin, and Rabbi Zavda, son-in-law of Rabbi Levi [said]: The all-Merciful [God] never exacts retribution against a person himself initially. From whom do you learn this? From Job, as it is stated: “There came a messenger to Job, and said: ‘The oxen were plowing [and the donkeys grazing beside them; and Sheba fell upon them, and took them; they smote the servants by sword; and only I by myself escaped to tell you]’” (Job 1:14–15). Rabbi Ḥama ben Rabbi Ḥanina said: The Holy One blessed be He showed…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:47, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Ruth Rabbah 2:10) to illuminate his teaching here (“In the Midrash Ruth Rabbah 2:10: “And the woman was left of her two children” Ruth 1:5—like the remnants shirei of meal-offerings. The Turei Zahav Taz, Yoreh De'ah 43:3 wrote that “remnants” shirayim denotes strictly...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And thus evil, inasmuch as it nests within the hearts of the Children of Israel, siphons its vitality from Hashem, blessed be He, because the Children of Israel are bound to Him. And therefore it was said, "And Sheba fell upon them and took them", regarding those "oxen plowing and she-asses feeding beside them", concerning which our Sages explained (Bava Batra 15b) that Hashem gave Job a taste of the World to Come—analogous to Shabbat being "a semblance of the World to Come" (Berakhot 57a), which channels worldly pleasures for the sake of Heaven.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Beshalach 10:3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: The expression “his name” teaches of will, for even shmo, “his name,” is numerically equivalent to “ratson,” “will” (both equal 346) as is mentioned in the Midrash (Bereshit Rabba, 34:11). The tsaddikim control their wills and consider their thoughts. If they deem them improper they refrain. With the wicked it is the opposite as their hearts possess them.It is written in the Midrash (Yalkut B’shalach 241 in the name of the Midrash Avchir), “the angel of Egypt came to recommend that God be merciful with them, so the angel Gavriel came with a brick, placed it before the Holy One, blessed be He, and said, ‘with this Egypt has subjected Israel to slave labor.’

The Turei Zahav Taz, Yoreh De'ah 43:3 wrote that “remnants” shirayim denotes strictly...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: In contrast, in kedushah one is consecrated unto Heaven, just as regarding betrothal (kiddushin) of a woman, our Rabbis explained in Kiddushin (2b): it is an expression of consecration (hekdesh), designating her exclusively to her husband. And the essence of song emerges from intense, passionate longing, which is why love-ballads are termed shirei agavim; and when a person's soul yearns away entirely toward Hashem, blessed be He, and he is lovesick for Him, then his mouth is opened to sing before Him.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Balak 9:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And behold, a man of the children of Israel came and brought close to his brethren a woman of Midian before Moshe and before the whole community of Israel .…” (Bamidbar, 25:6)Before his punishment he was called “a man of the children of Israel” and afterwards he is called “a man of Israel [verse 14].” This man said to Moshe, “who said Yitro’s daughter is permitted to you?

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 43:3: “Commenting on the laws of remnants (shirayim) in Yoreh De’ah 43:3, the Turei Zahav (Taz) explains that the term ‘remnant’ (shirayim) applies only to the minor portion left over after the majority has been removed.” Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:47, Rav Tzadok draws upon this commentary and philosophical-halakhic exposition (Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 43:3) to illuminate his teaching here (“The Turei Zahav Taz, Yoreh De'ah 43:3 wrote that “remnants” shirayim denotes strictly less than half; and I challenged him from the meal-offering, where only a handful kometz is burned while the majority remains, and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Sefer HaZikhronot, Mitzvot, Positive Commandment 2, Chapter 1 7 (§3)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And if he was born partially circumcised — a small part uncovered and the majority covered — his law is like one not circumcised properly from the start. Furthermore, even if he was born completely circumcised and afterwards skin grew or stretched over — the Turei Zahav [Taz] doubted whether his status is like one who was circumcised and then pulled back, where it requires complete coverage and only a rabbinic fix; or perhaps since he never underwent actual circumcision, having had no foreskin previously, and now having one — the biblical obligation returns; and he left this ruling undecided.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Exodus, Ki Tisa 1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Concerning the half-shekel (machatzit ha-shekel): as taught in Kiddushin 40b, ‘A person should always view himself as half-guilty and half-meritorious; when he performs a single mitzvah, happy is he for tipping himself and the entire world to the side of merit.’ Therefore ‘the rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than the half-shekel’—neither falling into haughtiness nor sinking into despair.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ruth 1:6: ‘She started out with her daughters-in-law to return from the country of Moab; for in the country of Moab she had heard that GOD had taken note of the people [of Israel] and given them food.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:48, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Ruth 1:6) to illuminate his teaching here (““For she had heard in the country of Moab how that Hashem had visited His people...” Ruth 1:6—from traveling peddlers who make the rounds through the towns. This can be explained via Bava Kamma 82a: Ezra instituted...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Novellae, Rif, Berachot 1:4
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Folio 6b, s.v. Rabbi Abbahu: "And it is an unresolved doubt of biblical law (teiku de'oraita)." – [Note]: This requires study, for the reading of the Torah on Mondays and Thursdays is only an enactment of Moses and Ezra as detailed in Bava Kamma [82a]. – And subsequently I heard that Ma'adanei Yom Tov [sec. 36, letter 9] sensed this, resolving: an enactment of the prophets is treated like biblical law.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Korach 8
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “… you have killed the people of God.” (Bamidbar, 17:6)Truly, the people knew that this act had come from God, yet their claim was God visited upon them because Moshe and Aharon hated them. This is why Moshe Rabeynu said to Aharon, “take the incense censer [to stop the plague],” to show the people God’s great love for them.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Kamma 82a: ‘§ The Sages taught that Ezra the Scribe instituted ten ordinances: He instituted that communities read the Torah on Shabbat in the afternoon; and they also read the Torah on every Monday and Thursday; and the courts convene and judge every Monday and Thursday; and one does laundry on Thursday; and one eats garlic on Shabbat eve. And Ezra further instituted that a woman should rise early and bake bread on those days when she wants to bake; and that a woman should don a breechcloth; and that a woman should first comb her hair and only then immerse in a ritual bath after being ritually impure; and that peddlers of cosmetics and perfumes should travel around through all the towns. And Ezra…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:48, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Kamma 82a) to illuminate his teaching here (“This can be explained via Bava Kamma 82a: Ezra instituted that peddlers travel among the towns selling cosmetics so wives would not be repulsive to their husbands; and the Sages taught Ta'anit 11a: marital intimacy...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And any subtle partition between upper and lower waters is designated a hairsbreadth: above, regarding the reception of divine flow, the distinction manifests in that a eunuch (saris) has no beard; while below, regarding the actual issuance of the flow, it is like a garlic peel, as stated at the end of chapter Merubbeh (Bava Kamma 82a) that garlic increases seed, and the garlic peel forms the partition [wherefore Ben Azzai said: "All the sages of Israel are like a garlic peel compared to me, except for the bald one [Rabbi Akiva]" (Bekhorot 58a).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Leviticus, Kedoshim 3:2
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: They will take care that where there is benefit derived in this world it should be done with a settled mind, and not in a state of panic. This is seen in the signs of pure birds as explained in the Gemara (Chullin, 65a), “a bird which seizes its prey is impure,” meaning that it does not have trust in God, so therefore all that it eats it clutches in its claws (for fear that it would lose it).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Taanit 11a: ‘Rav Yehuda said that Rav said: Anyone who has food for himself but nevertheless starves himself in years of famine will be saved from an unusual death, as it is stated: “In famine, He will redeem you from death” (Job 5:20). This is derived from the precise wording of the verse. According to its straightforward meaning, instead of “in famine,” it should have said: From famine, as one is delivered from famine. Rather, this is what the verse is saying: As a reward for starving himself in years of famine, Job will be saved from an unusual death.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:48, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Taanit 11a) to illuminate his teaching here (“and the Sages taught Ta'anit 11a: marital intimacy is forbidden during years of famine—so the arrival of peddlers was the unmistakable signal that the famine had ended:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And even regarding necessary sustenance, they stated: "He who sits in fasting is called holy" (Ta'anit 11a) [unlike one who perceives the Holy One abiding within his innards, meaning his inward organs are pure holiness, who is forbidden to fast (Ta'anit 11b), which is the level of Da'at as noted above]. Nevertheless, after reciting a blessing, having accepted the yoke of Heaven through Awe and straightforward Wisdom, "the earth He gave to the children of men" to derive physical enjoyment.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 4:5
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: However, he is not to separate from the prohibition at a time when he remembers that it is forbidden, for it is forbidden for him to separate himself based on this kind of counsel unless it a direct commandment from the blessed One. This is the explanation of the Gemara, “all who congratulate Yehuda,” meaning for one who thinks that it always proper to do as Yehuda did, is called a compromiser (or one who compromises with the Torah), for even Yehuda used such advice only at a time of testing.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ruth 1:7: ‘Accompanied by her two daughters-in-law, she left the place where she had been living; and they set out on the road back to the land of Judah.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:49, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Ruth 1:7) to illuminate his teaching here (““And they went on the way” Ruth 1:7—they set forth on a festival day Ruth Rabbah 2:12; for the Midrash was troubled: why specify “to return unto the land of Judah”? it clarifies that they walked on Yom Tov, and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For whom do we possess of higher pedigree than High Priests and Davidic monarchs? Yet every High Priest of the First Temple descended from Eleazar who married the daughters of Putiel (Jethro, Bava Batra 109b); and all kings of the House of David descended from Ruth the Moabitess, as did Isaiah; and writing "Ezekiel" was a scribal error for "Jeremiah," who was among the eight priestly prophets descending from Rahab (Megillah 14b).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Noach 2:2
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: This is the meaning of the verse, “the raven went back and forth until the waters dried from the land,” in other words, when evil lusts are eradicated there will be no need for anger, for water represents lust. Therefore in the Holy Temple there was a small hint of this, for there was an “ama caleh oreiv” (Mishna Middot, 4:6), a sharpened plate on the roof one cubit high that prevented ravens from roosting there (representing the eventual eradication of anger).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ruth Rabbah 2:12: ‘“She departed from the place where she had been, and her two daughters-in-law with her; they went on the way to return to the land of Judah” (Ruth 1:7).“She departed from the place where she had been.” “She departed” – was it she alone who departed from there? Did not several camel drivers depart, several donkey drivers depart, and you say “she departed”? Rabbi Azarya in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Simon [said]: The most prominent person in the city, he is its radiance, he is its splendor, he is its glory, and he is its praise. When he vacates it, its radiance vacates, its splendor vacates, its glory vacates, and its praise vacates. So you find with Jacob our patriarch when he…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:49, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Ruth Rabbah 2:12) to illuminate his teaching here (““And they went on the way” Ruth 1:7—they set forth on a festival day Ruth Rabbah 2:12; for the Midrash was troubled: why specify “to return unto the land of Judah”? it clarifies that they walked on Yom Tov, and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is the essential superiority of Israel: that they possess genealogical lineage; as the Sages stated (Bamidbar Rabbah 9:7): Hashem said to the nations, "Bring Me the book of genealogies as My children bring!"; unlike the idolaters: "a people resembling a donkey" (Bereishis 22:5; Yevamos 62a), where there is no legal paternity for a gentile to trace after the father's family (Yevamos 98a), being like an animal that possesses no lineage; and therefore Scripture said: "Gad, a troop shall march upon his heels" (Bereishis 49:19), for those who went forth in the troop in the wars of the House of David were genealogically certified, as written in Kiddushin (76b).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayigash 1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: When Judah approached Joseph and when Jacob sent Judah ahead of him to Goshen “to establish a house of study for him” (Bereshit Rabbah 95:3): the conjunction of Judah and Joseph unites the heartfelt brokenness and repentance of Judah with the steadfast covenantal purity of Joseph, establishing the enduring house of Torah even within the exile of Egypt.

Did not several camel drivers depart, several donkey drivers depart, and you say “she departed”? Rabbi Azarya in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Rabbi Simon [said]: The most prominent person in the city, he is its radiance, he is its splendor, he is its glory, and he is its praise. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And therefore did not enter Eretz Yisrael because his level surpassed it. And as for us, since the destruction of the Temple, we have only the lowest rung of the shining of the face— meaning: the outer radiance of the Face, which is the Shechinah that went into exile with them, the spiritual level of 'Ani', meaning: that He dwells within his heart; namely that the perception itself is the very entity perceived, for he apprehends that no place is devoid of Him and 'the whole earth is full of His glory'—.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayera 6
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And Avraham journeyed from there to the land of the Negev.” (Bereshit, 20:1)Avraham Avinu refined all kinds of love in the world so that they be dedicated to God alone. Then, when he saw how an action as the incident between Lot and his two daughters could have occurred, he began anew the entire process of refining love. This is “and he journeyed,”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ruth 1:8: ‘But Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, “Turn back, each of you to her mother’s house. May GOD deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me!’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:50, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Ruth 1:8) to illuminate his teaching here (““With me” Ruth 1:8—teaching that the daughters-in-law waived their marriage contracts ketubah to Naomi Ruth Rabbah 2:13; the traditional commentary Matnot Kehunah explains that Naomi had acted as a guarantor for...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Just as occurred in the purchase of the birthright. And all divine services of our father Jacob, peace be upon him, centered on wealth, property, and 'with all your might'. And the trial of King David, peace be upon him, was in the realm of desire, which is the attribute of Malchut in the intensity of desire, built from the deep desires of the feminine: Lot's daughters, Tamar, and Ruth.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Deuteronomy, Nitzavim 5
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And you shall return unto the Lord your God, and hearken to His voice… And you shall return and hearken to the voice of the Lord” (Deuteronomy 30:2, 8). Corresponding to the Zohar’s teaching on the ascending levels of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah (Zohar II:94b), each stage of teshuvah elevates a person to a higher capacity of hearing the Divine voice—first purifying his deeds, and then illuminating the depths of his heart.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Ruth Rabbah 2:13: ‘“Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law: Go, return each woman to her mother's house; may the Lord perform kindness with you, as you performed with the dead, and with me” (Ruth 1:8).“Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law: Go, return each woman to her mother's house [beit immah]” – to the house of her nation [beit ummatah]. The mother of Avnimos the weaver died, and Rabbi Meir ascended to pay his respects and found them sitting in mourning. Later, his father died, and Rabbi Meir ascended to pay his respects and found them engaged in their labor. He said to him: ‘It appears to me that your mother was dearer to you than your father.’ He said to him: ‘But is it not written so: “Each…to her…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:50, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Ruth Rabbah 2:13) to illuminate his teaching here (““With me” Ruth 1:8—teaching that the daughters-in-law waived their marriage contracts ketubah to Naomi Ruth Rabbah 2:13; the traditional commentary Matnot Kehunah explains that Naomi had acted as a guarantor for...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And since both spiritual levels were integrated within them in absolute unity, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel debated from which dimension consummate satisfaction and spiritual rest (neichah) is derived. Now, in our present reality where a person has not yet attained this supreme vantage [which was the rare level of Rabbi Meir, and not every person merits it], the Gemara advises: "Let him examine his deeds" (yefashpesh), etc.; one requires painstaking scrutiny of actions, which consists of boundaries and halachic borders: "this you shall perform" and "this you shall not do".
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Toldot 1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And these are the generations of Yitzchak, son of Avraham: Avraham begot Yitzchak” (Genesis 25:19). Scripture states: “Know the God of your father and serve Him with a whole heart; if you seek Him, He will be found by you” (I Chronicles 28:9). Abraham represents the initial awakening of chessed given from Above, whereas Isaac represents the arduous inner labor of fear and self-refinement through which a person makes that divine illumination his own permanent acquisition.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And it seems to me that regarding brothers of a man whose sons died — all agree no hazardous presumption extends to him. If I were to say: I have hope, even were I to be with a husband tonight, and also were I to bear sons” (Ruth 1:12).“Turn back, my daughters, go” – Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said in the name of Rabbi Yudan bar Rabbi Ḥanina: In three places it is written here: “Turn back” (Ruth 1:8), “Turn back” (Ruth 1:11), “Turn back” (Ruth 1:12), corresponding to the three times that one rejects a convert.
